ch21.note: The Loyal and Patriotic Army (忠义救国军, Zhōngyì Jiùguójūn) was a guerrilla and irregular force raised from 1938 by Dai Li’s secret service in the Shanghai–Jiangsu–Zhejiang region. Nominally a resistance army, it doubled as a behind-the-lines arm of the Juntong; its Shanghai office, as here, partly served as cover for District work.

ch21.anchor: soon to be joined in marriage
ch21.note: The original phrase, jié wéi Qín-Jìn (结为秦晋), invokes the intermarriages between the ruling houses of the states of Qin and Jin in the Spring and Autumn period; “a match of Qin and Jin” has been the set expression for a marriage alliance between two families ever since.

The Shanghai foreign authorities, above all the International Settlement, built and policed roads beyond their treaty limits into the surrounding Chinese districts. These “extra-settlement roads” (越界筑路, yuèjiè zhùlù) lay in a legal gray zone of disputed jurisdiction, which by 1939 let the Japanese and their puppets operate along them more freely than inside the concessions proper.

A tingzijian (亭子间, literally “pavilion room”) is the small, cheap room over the kitchen and off the stair landing of a Shanghai lane house, a fixture of the city’s cramped middle-class housing and, in the 1930s, proverbially the lodging of struggling writers and clerks.

Bǎixiàngrén (白相人) is Shanghai dialect for an idler or man-about-town, commonly a petty tough who lived by his wits on the edge of the underworld. The white shirt and glossy black trousers Zheng notes were the type’s recognized get-up.

The fabi (法币, “legal tender”) was the paper currency the Nationalist government made China’s sole legal money in 1935. Wartime issue drove it into steep inflation, so a courier’s thirty-eight yuan a month, meagre to begin with, bought steadily less; Chen sets the figure down to mark how poor his people were kept.

Tang Shengzhi (唐生智, 1889–1970), a Hunanese general who rose under the Nationalists and more than once rebelled against Chiang Kai-shek; the rising meant here is one of his anti-Chiang revolts around 1929–30. He later commanded the doomed defense of Nanjing in 1937.

Deng Yanda (邓演达, 1895–1931), a leading left-wing Nationalist, was seized by Chiang Kai-shek’s agents and secretly executed in 1931; the “Deng Yanda affair” refers to that operation. The “Two Guangs affair” (两广事件) was the June 1936 revolt of the Guangdong and Guangxi militarists against Nanjing. Chen means that Wu Naixian had a hand in the secret-service side of both.
